The Mountain sucker (Catostomus platyrhynchus) is a relatively small-bodied catostomid endemic to cold-water streams of the western United States and Canada. Individuals reach a maximum total length of 25 cm [Li = 25 cm], a modest size compared to many of its congeners, though substantial for a species occupying high-elevation, oligotrophic habitats. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to this length is 131.7 grams [Wwi = 131.7 grams], placing the species among the smaller members of the genus Catostomus. Field surveys and growth curve analyses indicate that this asymptotic mass is achieved only after several years of slow, sustained growth, likely constrained by the low productivity of the cold, snowmelt-driven systems the fish inhabits. In contrast, the total length at puberty is only 11 cm [Lp = 11 cm], meaning that individuals begin the transition to reproductive maturity when they have achieved less than half of their ultimate length. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is 10.4 grams [Wwp = 10.4 grams], a value that underscores the substantial energetic investment required for the adult soma to reach its full size. This disparity between size at first maturation and maximum size suggests a life-history strategy in which early reproduction is favored despite the potential costs to continued somatic growth.

Newly hatched Mountain suckers emerge from the egg as yolk-dependent larvae, having exhausted a maternally provisioned nutrient reserve contained within the fertilised ovum. That minute body mass, equivalent to only a few milligrams, reflects the lecithotrophic strategy of the alevin stage, during which the larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk before the onset of exogenous feeding. The transition to active feeding, marked by mouth opening and first prey capture, occurs once yolk-sac resorption nears completion, a point at which the young fish weighs just a small fraction of a gram. The timing of this trophic switch is critical, as the point of no return is rapidly approached if suitable planktonic prey are not encountered soon after the completion of yolk absorption. This exceptionally low birth mass, combined with the protracted growth to puberty, implies that the larval and early juvenile periods are likely periods of high mortality risk.

A comparative perspective reveals that the life-history parameters of Catostomus platyrhynchus align closely with those of other cold-water catostomids, though some notable differences emerge. The ultimate length of 25 cm [Li = 25 cm] is somewhat smaller than that reported for the closely related Catostomus catostomus, which can exceed 30 cm, but is consistent with the size of species confined to high-gradient, oligotrophic streams. The wet weight corresponding to this asymptotic length, 131.7 grams [Wwi = 131.7 grams], reflects the relatively slender body form characteristic of the genus. The reproductive strategy, in which females attaining just 11 cm [Lp = 11 cm] in total length begin to mature, with a corresponding wet weight at puberty of 10.4 grams [Wwp = 10.4 grams], suggests a life history that prioritises early reproduction under the constraints of a short growing season and limited food availability. The birth mass of 0.0036 grams [Wwb = 0.0036 grams] is typical of catostomids that produce large numbers of small, demersal eggs that are broadcast over gravel substrates. When combined, these traits paint a picture of a relatively slow-living fish with a conservative reproductive schedule, well matched to the unproductive, cold environments it inhabits.
